Prepared by Prof. Leon Zolotoy

What this glossary covers: recap of risk-return trade-off under CAPM and the concept of Treynor ratio as the measure of reward to systematic risk ratio; the concept of style (factor) investing and commonly employed value, size, momentum, and defensive style investing strategies; the concept of factor models and the use of factor models in investment fund-performance evaluation.

1Risk-return trade-offRisk-return and CAPM recap

Stocks with higher risk on average offer higher returns. A typical investor prefers higher returns and lower risk, but there is no “free lunch” on financial markets.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Higher returns over lower returnsA typical investor would prefer higher returns over lower returns.
Lower risk over higher riskA typical investor would prefer lower risk over higher risk.
Firm-specific riskRisk related to firm-specific events; it can be reduced by creating diversified portfolios of stocks.
Systematic riskRisk related to market-wide events; it remains after firm-specific events are diversified away.
Market risk premiumThe compensation investors receive, on average, for exposure to systematic market risk.
Example
Diversification and remaining risk

As the number of stocks in a portfolio increases, portfolio standard deviation declines because risk related to firm-specific events is washed out.

Market-wide events still affect the portfolio, leaving exposure to systematic risk.

2Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)Risk-return and CAPM recap

A model in which the mean (expected) return on investment is given by the risk-free rate plus beta multiplied by the market risk premium.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Risk-free rateThe return on a risk-free investment, denoted by rf.
BetaA measure of systematic risk; in CAPM it measures sensitivity to the market portfolio.
Market risk premiumThe mean (expected) return on the market portfolio in excess of the risk-free rate.
Portfolio mean returnThe weighted average of mean returns on individual stocks in the portfolio.
Portfolio betaThe weighted average of individual stock betas in the portfolio.
Formula and formula components
CAPM expected return
E(ri) = rf + βi[E(rm) − rf]
Formula componentSymbol / itemExplanation
Mean expected returnE(ri)Expected return on investment i.
Risk-free raterfReturn on a risk-free investment.
BetaβiSensitivity of investment i to the market portfolio.
Market risk premiumE(rm) − rfExpected return on the market portfolio in excess of the risk-free rate.
Beta
βi = Cov(ri, rm)Var(rm)
Formula componentSymbol / itemExplanation
Covariance with marketCov(ri, rm)Co-movement of investment returns with market returns.
Variance of market returnsVar(rm)Total variation in market portfolio returns.
Portfolio mean return and beta (a 3-stock portfolio example)
E(rp) = wAE(rA) + wBE(rB) + wCE(rC)
βp = wAβA + wBβB + wCβC
Formula componentSymbol / itemExplanation
Portfolio weightswA, wB, wCWeights invested in stocks A, B, and C.
Stock expected returnsE(rA), E(rB), E(rC)Mean returns on stocks A, B, and C.
Stock betasβA, βB, βCIndividual stock sensitivities to the market portfolio.
Numerical example
Portfolio mean return and portfolio beta

A portfolio invests 45% in stock A, 20% in stock B, and 35% in stock C. The mean returns are 7.45%, 8.24%, and 8.65%; the betas are 0.91, 1.12, and 1.43.

Portfolio mean return = 0.45×7.45% + 0.20×8.24% + 0.35×8.65% = 8.028%. Portfolio beta = 0.45×0.91 + 0.20×1.12 + 0.35×1.43 = 1.134.

3Treynor ratioRisk-return and CAPM recap

Expected excess return per unit of systematic risk; expected reward adjusted to systematic market risk.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Expected excess returnExpected return on investment minus the risk-free rate.
Systematic riskMeasured by beta in the CAPM framework.
Same Treynor ratioThe message of CAPM is that all investments should have the same expected excess return per unit of systematic risk.
Formula and formula components
Treynor ratio
Treynorp = E(rp) − rfβp
Formula componentSymbol / itemExplanation
Treynor ratioTreynorpExpected excess return per unit of beta for portfolio p.
Expected portfolio returnE(rp)Mean expected return on portfolio p.
Risk-free raterfRisk-free rate used to calculate excess return.
Portfolio betaβpSensitivity of portfolio returns to market portfolio returns.
Numerical example
Style investing prelude

Portfolios A–D have different average monthly returns and betas. With a monthly risk-free rate of 0.18%, the monthly Treynor ratio is average return minus the risk-free rate divided by beta.

Portfolio B has the highest Treynor ratio in this example: (0.97 − 0.18) ÷ 0.78 = 1.013.

=SLOPE(A6:A362,$E$6:$E$362)

4Style (factor) investingStyle investing framework and core style strategies

An investment approach based on the idea that some stocks may have higher expected reward adjusted for market risk (ie: higher Treynor ratio) and can be identified based on certain stock characteristics or styles.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Stock characteristic / styleA stock attribute used to divide stocks into groups and compare performance.
Value, momentum, defensive, size, and mixThe prominent types of style investing shown in the material.
Smart beta investingFocusing on stocks with selected characteristics—such as value, low volatility, or past winning performance—rather than investing only according to the weights of a broad market index.
Smart beta investment fundsInvestment funds closely related to style investing that give higher portfolio weight to stocks with characteristics that, on average, have outperformed the market.
Example
Morningstar Ratings

Morningstar first sorts investment funds into groups based on their investment style, such as small-cap versus large-cap stocks and value versus growth stocks. It then ranks each fund’s prior performance relative to peer funds in the same group: five stars indicate top past performers, while one star indicates bottom past performers.

Back to top
5Value investingStyle investing framework and core style strategies

An approach that focuses on identifying stocks that are presumed to be underpriced relative to their intrinsic value, so that market price is presumed to be too low compared to firm fundamentals.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Value stocksStocks presumed to be underpriced relative to intrinsic value.
High book-to-market ratioA common value identifier; book value of equity divided by market value of equity.
Low price-to-earnings ratioA common value identifier; market price of a stock divided by earnings per share.
Low EV/CFO ratioA common value identifier; enterprise value divided by cash flow from operations.
High dividend yieldA common value identifier; dividend per share divided by market price of a stock.
Value premiumThe tendency of high book-to-market ratio stocks to outperform, on average, low book-to-market ratio stocks.
Formula and formula components
Value identifiers
Book-to-market = Book value of equityMarket value of equity
Dividend yield = Dividend per shareMarket price of a stock
Formula componentSymbol / itemExplanation
Book value of equityBook value of equityAccounting value of shareholders’ equity.
Market value of equityMarket value of equityEquity value implied by market prices.
Dividend per shareDividend per shareDividend paid for each share.
Market price of a stockMarket priceCurrent market price of a stock.
Numerical example
Value investing in-class exercise results

Five groups are sorted by prior-period book-to-market ratio. Group 1 contains low book-to-market stocks and Group 5 contains high book-to-market stocks.

In the results, Group 5 has a higher average monthly return and a higher Treynor ratio than Group 1.

6Size-based investingStyle investing framework and core style strategies

An approach that classifies stocks into groups based on their market capitalization, or size.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Market capitalizationNumber of shares outstanding multiplied by market price of a stock.
Small cap stocksStocks of firms with low market capitalization.
Large cap stocksStocks of firms with high market capitalization.
Formula and formula components
Market capitalization
Market capitalization = Number of shares outstanding × Market price of a stock
Formula componentSymbol / itemExplanation
Number of shares outstandingNumber of shares outstandingTotal number of shares issued by the firm.
Market price of a stockMarket priceCurrent market price of one share.
Numerical example
Size-based investing in-class exercise results

Five groups are sorted by prior-period market capitalization. Group 1 contains small-cap stocks and Group 5 contains large-cap stocks.

In the results, the small-cap group has a higher average monthly return and a higher Treynor ratio than the large-cap group.

7Defensive equity investingStyle investing framework and core style strategies

An approach that focuses on stocks with low risk, measured by low return volatility or low CAPM beta.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Low return volatilityA commonly used metric for low risk.
Low CAPM betaA measure of low systematic risk in the CAPM framework.
Low risk anomaliesThe tendency of low-risk stocks to deliver higher average returns per unit of risk.
Sorting based on stock return volatilityStocks are grouped from low return volatility to high return volatility.
Sorting based on betaStocks are grouped from low beta to high beta.
Numerical example
Defensive equity investing results

The analysis sorts stocks into five groups using two methods: prior-period stock return volatility and prior-period stock beta.

In both sorts, the low-risk group has a higher Treynor ratio than the high-risk group.

8Momentum investingStyle investing framework and core style strategies

An approach that focuses on stocks with good past performance, where past winning stocks tend to continue being winners.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Past “winning” stocksStocks with the best past 12-month returns.
Past “loser” stocksStocks with the worst past 12-month returns.
Past 12-month returnsThe sorting variable used in the in-class exercise.
Momentum across different stock marketsThe tendency of past winners to outperform past losers is a global pattern.
Numerical example
Momentum investing in-class exercise results

Five groups are sorted by past stock performance. Group 1 contains past loser stocks and Group 5 contains past winner stocks.

In the results, the past winner group has a higher average monthly return and a higher Treynor ratio than the past loser group.

9Long position / short positionStyle investing returns and risk

An investment strategy in which an investor 1) buys a stock believed to be underpriced, betting that later the stock price will “correct itself” and go up and 2) borrows and sells a stock believed to be overpriced, betting that later the stock price will “correct itself” and go down.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Long positionBuying a stock that is believed to be underpriced.
Short positionBorrowing and selling a stock that is believed to be overpriced.
Underpriced stockA stock whose market price is believed to be too low.
Overpriced stockA stock whose market price is believed to be too high.
Example
Style-based long-short trade

If an investor believes value stocks are underpriced and growth stocks are overpriced, the investor may buy value stocks and sell short growth stocks. The key question is whether this investment strategy, on average, delivers superior risk-adjusted returns or increases an investor’s exposure to risk.

10Style investing returns and riskStyle investing returns and risk

The idea that superior returns from style investing may capture risk rather than purely mispricing.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Worsening economic and financial market conditionsValue and small-cap stocks tend to be more vulnerable to these conditions.
Risks not captured by CAPMSome evidence suggests that momentum and low-risk anomalies may reflect risks not captured by CAPM.
Sharp drawdownA large decline in investment value that can occur when factor returns come with risk.
Prolonged periods of underperformanceA risk that style investing can underperform for extended periods.
Example
Style investing during the Global Financial Crisis

Returns on portfolios sorted by size and book-to-market ratio during the Global Financial Crisis period of 2008–2009 illustrate that style portfolios can experience material losses.

This supports the interpretation that at least part of style investing performance may reflect compensation for risk.

11Factor modelsFactor models

Models in which systematic risk is driven by risk factors and betas measure stock sensitivity to those risk factors; part of return is due to firm-specific events.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Systematic newsNews that affects all stocks.
Firm-specific newsNews specific to a particular firm.
Risk factorsVariables that drive systematic risk in the factor model.
Factor betasMeasures of stock sensitivity to risk factors.
Firm-specific componentThe part of return due to firm-specific events.
CAPM as a single-factor modelCAPM has one risk factor: market risk factor.
Formula and formula components
General factor model
ri − rf = αi + βi,1F1 + βi,2F2 + … + βi,KFK + εi
Formula componentSymbol / itemExplanation
Excess returnri − rfInvestment return minus the risk-free rate.
AlphaαiRisk-adjusted return after controlling for risk factors.
Factor betaβi,kSensitivity of investment i to risk factor k.
Risk factorFkA source of systematic risk.
Firm-specific componentεiPart of return not explained by the risk factors.
Example
Market factor versus additional factors

CAPM treats the market risk factor as the only factor that matters and therefore is, effectively, a single-factor model. Models with multiple factors introduce a natural extension to CAPM, allowing for additional factors, on top of the market risk factor, to be included.

12Style-based risk factorsFactor models

Risk factors constructed from style portfolios, added on top of the market factor if style investing returns capture risk rather than mispricing.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Value factor (HML)Return on high book-to-market ratio stocks portfolio minus return on low book-to-market ratio stocks portfolio.
Size factor (SMB)Return on small-cap stocks portfolio minus return on large-cap stocks portfolio.
Momentum factor (MOM)Return on past winner stocks portfolio minus return on past loser stocks portfolio.
Ongoing debate about momentumThere is ongoing debate as to whether momentum captures risk or mispricing.
Formula and formula components
Style factor construction
HML = rhigh book-to-market − rlow book-to-market
SMB = rsmall-cap − rlarge-cap
MOM = rpast winners − rpast losers
Formula componentSymbol / itemExplanation
HMLHMLHigh-minus-low value factor.
SMBSMBSmall-minus-big size factor.
MOMMOMMomentum factor based on past winners minus past losers.

A popular factor model that adds size and value risk factors to the market risk factor.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Three factorsMarket risk factor, size factor, and value factor.
Regression alphaRisk-adjusted return after controlling for the three factors.
Factor betasSensitivities to the market, SMB, and HML factors.
Formula and formula components
Fama/French 3-factor model
ri − rf = αi + βMKT,i(rm − rf) + βSMB,iSMB + βHML,iHML + εi
Formula componentSymbol / itemExplanation
Excess investment returnri − rfReturn on investment i minus the risk-free rate.
AlphaαiRisk-adjusted return after controlling for the factors included in the model.
Market risk factorrm − rfReturn on the market portfolio minus the risk-free rate.
Size factor (SMB)SMBReturn on the small-cap stocks portfolio minus return on the large-cap stocks portfolio.
Value factor (HML)HMLReturn on the high book-to-market ratio stocks portfolio minus return on the low book-to-market ratio stocks portfolio.
Market betaβMKT,iSensitivity of the return on investment i to the market risk factor.
Size betaβSMB,iSensitivity of the return on investment i to the size factor (SMB).
Value betaβHML,iSensitivity of the return on investment i to the value factor (HML).
Firm-specific componentεiThe part of the return on investment i due to firm-specific events.

15Factor models and investment performanceInvestment performance evaluation

A regression-based approach to evaluating risk-adjusted investment performance by separating portfolio-manager skill from the risk profile of an investment.

Key subterms
Key subterm / itemExplanation
Attribution problemHow to separate portfolio-manager skill from the impact of risk factors.
Dependent variableReturn on investment fund minus risk-free rate.
Independent variablesRisk factors prescribed by the model.
AlphaThe regression intercept; it measures risk-adjusted return after controlling for risk factors.
BetasRegression slopes measuring sensitivity of investment return to each risk factor.
Investment styles of the fund managerInsights inferred from the fund’s factor betas.
Numerical example
Factor model example: Fund A and Fund B

The data sheet calculates each fund’s return in excess of the risk-free rate and then uses regression analysis to estimate alpha and factor betas.

Statistical significance is assessed using t-statistics: a coefficient is treated as statistically significant when the absolute value of its t-statistic exceeds 1.96. The interpretation below focuses on alpha and the non-market factor betas.

Interpretation of the regression estimates

Fund A
EstimateCoefficientt-statisticInterpretation
Alpha−0.0002−0.250Statistically insignificant: no evidence the fund has delivered positive (or negative) risk-adjusted returns.
Size factor (SMB) beta0.709720.105Beta > 0 and statistically significant: focuses on small-cap stocks.
Value factor (HML) beta0.673528.395Beta > 0 and statistically significant: focuses on “value” stocks (stocks with high book-to-market ratio).
Momentum factor (MOM) beta−0.0454−1.616Beta not significant: no evidence of focus on past stock performance.
Fund B
EstimateCoefficientt-statisticInterpretation
Alpha0.00030.378Statistically insignificant: no evidence the fund has delivered positive (or negative) risk-adjusted returns.
Size factor (SMB) beta−0.1742−5.205Beta < 0 and statistically significant: focuses on large-cap stocks.
Value factor (HML) beta−0.0583−2.594Beta < 0 and statistically significant: focuses on “growth” stocks (stocks with low book-to-market ratio).
